title: Puff stitch
subtitle: Elongated half trebles pulled together into a soft raised oval
excerpt: The puff stitch pulls multiple elongated half treble loops into the same stitch, then closes them all together. The result is a softer, rounder texture than a bobble — less defined, more cushioned. Common in floral motifs and baby-weight accessories.
sourceNotes: Puff stitch technique synthesised from Weldon's Practical Crochet textured stitch descriptions (Internet Archive) and standard modern crochet teaching convention for the half-treble-based puff.
heroPrompt: A crochet swatch showing puff stitches in cream DK cotton, the soft oval puffs sitting among rows of double crochet, soft daylight from the side showing the height of the puffs.

glossaryTerms.definition: Multiple elongated half treble loops pulled into the same stitch and closed together with a single yarn over. Softer than a bobble, less defined than a popcorn. Works from a half treble base rather than a treble base.

content.text: uses the half treble as its building block, not the full treble. You yarn over, insert, pull up a tall loop — and instead of finishing the stitch, you repeat that three-step sequence three to five more times into the same stitch. The result is a cluster of tall unfinished loops, which you then close with one final yarn over through everything. The fabric effect is rounder and softer than a bobble.
Yarn over, insert the hook into the next stitch, yarn over again and pull up a loop approximately 1 cm tall — taller than a normal loop. Three loops on hook.
Yarn over, insert hook into the SAME stitch again, yarn over, pull up another tall loop. Five loops on hook.
Repeat step 2 three more times (for a 5-loop puff). Eleven loops on hook.
Yarn over and pull through all eleven loops at once. One loop remains. The puff is closed.
Work ch 1 to lock and anchor the puff before continuing to the next stitch.

attrs.title: Loop height matters
attrs.body: Pull each loop up to the same height — about 1 cm for DK yarn. If the loops are pulled at different heights, the puff will be lopsided. A consistent pull height makes the puff round and even.

items.symptom: The puff is flat rather than rounded
items.cause: The loops were not pulled tall enough, so the cluster does not have enough bulk to push forward.
items.fix: Pull each loop up at least 1 cm — noticeably taller than a regular half treble loop. The exaggerated height is what creates the puff shape.

items.symptom: The stitch is too difficult to pull the final yarn over through
items.cause: Too many loops were added, or the tension became tight across later loops.
items.fix: Try a 3-loop or 4-loop puff as a starting point. Add more loops once the tension management is easy.

items.symptom: The fabric puckers badly around the puff
items.cause: The base stitch was too small to accept multiple insertions, or the closing ch 1 was omitted.
items.fix: Always work the locking ch 1 after the puff. If the fabric still puckers, place the puff into a chain space rather than a regular stitch.

content.text: Puff stitches work beautifully in floral crochet motifs where they form the centre of a flower, surrounded by chains. Try five puffs arranged around a magic ring with ch 3 between each — that is a simple five-petal flower.
